name: Marine War Risk Insurance
summary: Marine war risk, Day 199. The premium never normalised (7.5–10% of hull since late July) and the September evidence — rationed US air cover, repeated UKMTO-logged hits including on the 'safe' Omani side, tanker rates at $1m/day — all points to cover tightening further, not easing; a fresh percentage print is the one data gap this sweep. The Red Sea leg (0.5–0.75% in July) now faces a Houthi-held Bab el-Mandeb and must reprice. Iran has explicitly weaponised the insurance mechanism via its 'restricted zone' sanctions list. Normalisation triggers (JWC delisting, sub-0.5–0.8% AWRP) are as far away as at any point in the war.

recent_signals.headline: **NO FRESH PREMIUM PRINT SINCE ~11 JULY — and the more important finding is that the market has shifted from a PRICE constraint to a CAPACITY constraint.** The 3-10% of hull / 'double-digit millions per trip' range stands, with US/UK/Israel-linked vessels at 2.5-5.0% versus 0.8-1.5% for non-flag-risk ships — roughly 3x, i.e. **flag and beneficial-ownership discrimination is now explicit underwriting policy** (pre-war baseline was 0.15-0.2%). But the binding mechanism is elsewhere: **underwriting capacity per VLCC transit has HALVED-to-QUARTERED from $2-3bn to $500m-$1.5bn, and 6 of 13 IG P&I clubs have withdrawn Gulf war cover.** The Lloyd's Market Association has separately argued that SAFETY concerns, not insurance availability, are driving reduced traffic — an important nuance meaning this is not yet a capacity crisis in the classic sense; cover is still being written, owners simply will not sail. **Forecasting implication: reopening requires an UNDERWRITING decision, not a diplomatic one, and underwriters price on observed loss experience — expect a 4-8 week lag after any ceasefire.** No JWC circular dated July; no delisting; listing framework confirmed only as of 3 March. REPORTED — do NOT assert an unprinted premium number.

**THE CAPACITY THESIS IS FALSIFIED ON THREE SEPARATE LEGS — this reverses the 19 July brief's central non-consensus call.** **(1) THE PREMIUM WENT DOWN, NOT UP.** The freshest hard figure is **Marsh — the SAME broker as the 28 June baseline — via Bloomberg on 9 July: 2-6% of VESSEL VALUE**, from a fraction of a percent pre-conflict; at the top of that range a $100m tanker costs $6m per transit. Marcus Baker, Marsh's Global Head of Marine, adds that at the conflict's height some ships paid **10%**, and that **before the July attacks rates had drifted BELOW 2%**. The 28 June figure was 3-8% of HULL. Same house, later date, lower range. **Carry 2-6% (Marsh, 9 Jul); flag 3-8% as superseded or basis-inconsistent.** **(2) THE P&I CLAIM IS A CATEGORY ERROR AND STALE.** Lloyd's List (David Osler, **4 March 2026**, LL1156515), headlined *'No, P&I clubs have not cancelled war risk cover'*, establishes that **war risk is a SEPARATE INSURANCE CLASS**: club rulebooks exclude it by design, owners buy annual hull war-risk separately, and IG excess war-risk cover and pooling 'stood as agreed.' The six-club episode (Gard, Skuld, NorthStandard, London P&I, American Club, Steamship Mutual) was a **1-5 MARCH** event driven by reinsurers pulling capacity; it explicitly did NOT affect mutual P&I or IG-pooled excess war cover; and gCaptain's 5 March follow-up ran *'Insurers Say War Cover Still Available for Gulf Voyages.'* **RETIRE the claim.** **(3) COVER IS AVAILABLE AND BEING WRITTEN.** WTW's Simon Lockwood, 9 Jul: 'requests for quotes has dropped off given a reluctance to commit to transits, although we are still receiving inquiries and **terms are available**.' **THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS OWNER AND CREW APPETITE, NOT UNDERWRITING CAPACITY** — which is what the Lloyd's Market Association said all along. **The '4-8 week reopening lag' was INFERRED, not sourced — retire it.** No July restatement of the '2-4 weeks of confirmed calm' formula exists. NEGATIVE FINDINGS: **no war-risk premium print newer than 9 July (12 days); no JWC circular located** (LMA 404, Lloyd's List 403 — absence-of-evidence, NOT a verified negative, and the single highest-value follow-up); no new P&I withdrawal in July. CONFIRMED.

**THE 21 JULY CORRECTION HELD ANOTHER CYCLE — Hormuz reopening is gated by CREW AND OWNER APPETITE, not underwriting capacity.** No war-risk premium print newer than the 9 July Marsh figure of 2-6% of vessel value has been published despite three-to-four ships struck since; all signals are qualitative ('surge again,' 'braces for prolonged elevated premiums'). NO new JWC listing change. NO ITF/IBF Warlike-Operations-Area declaration (STILL OVERDUE). The load-bearing datum remains labour: **Sinokor's six-months'-salary offer for one ~30-day Hormuz round trip was reconfirmed 21 July** and The National ran it as 'Danger money.' The market clears on seafarer refusal, not cover withdrawal — which is why transits collapsed to a trickle even though cover is available and priced. CONFIRMED (the absence of any print above 2-6%).

**THE CORRECTION HELD ANOTHER CYCLE — and a soft number must be rejected.** Despite 5-6 struck/attacked hulls across two theatres, there is STILL no war-risk premium print newer than the 9 July Marsh figure of 2-6% of vessel value (~14 days stale), no JWC listed-area circular, and no ITF/IBF Warlike-Operations-Area declaration (still OVERDUE). **REJECT the 'near-1,900% war-risk surge' number blanketing the tape: it traces to deVere Group CEO Nigel Green, a WEALTH-MANAGEMENT COMMENTATOR, describes a premium INCREASE not a percentage-of-hull rate, and is NOT a Marsh/WTW/JWC print — CLAIMED sentiment.** The binding constraint remains labour: Sinokor's six-months'-salary offer for one ~30-day Hormuz round trip stands.
